Enterprise UX · Product modernization

Modernizing Hardware
Virtualized I/O in PowerHMC

Re-examining complex infrastructure-management workflows from legacy interfaces toward a modern React and Carbon Design System experience.

My role
Product Designer
Contribution
Design ownership + collaboration
Timeline
Mar 2026 to now
Status
Ongoing, no shipped metrics yet

Enterprise software rarely fails on aesthetics. It fails because the person who has to act can't find the thing they need to act on.

The short version

What was wrong, what we did, how we knew

What was wrong

A blank page and a pile of pop-ups

The old screen showed nothing until you picked an item from a dropdown. Every change then opened a pop-up over the page you were on, and it never told you whether the change worked.

What we did

Show everything first, keep the page in view

  • Every network adapter listed up front in a table
  • A side panel, so the page stays in view
  • A page for each port
  • Clear feedback while loading, on success and on error

How we knew

We listened, then we changed things

I reviewed the old screens, talked to admins in four discovery sessions, and showed designs to them in three feedback sessions. Each design choice below points back to something a person said or did.

Context

IBM Power servers run banks, airlines and phone companies. The administrators who look after them spend their days in PowerHMC, a dense control panel. When something here is confusing, the cost is real.

The product

Trusted, and showing its age

PowerHMC has been around for years. Admins rely on it, and many of its screens were built long ago in a different style.

The challenge

Modernize, but don't break habits

The product was moving to a new look and technology. Our job was to improve the experience while keeping the tasks admins already know how to do.

My part

From first look to final build

I studied the old screens, sketched and designed the new ones, tested ideas with admins, made decisions with engineers, and checked the finished build.

Primer

First, a quick picture of how it all fits

PowerHMC is the control panel for a Power server. To understand "Hardware virtualized I/O", it helps to see who is connected to what.

The problem

So what was going wrong?

PowerHMC was being rebuilt on a newer technology (React and the Carbon Design System), one screen at a time. This was one of those screens, and it was a good time to ask whether it worked for the people using it.

Three things an admin would run into

01You see nothing until you ask

The page was empty until you picked an adapter from a dropdown. No overview, no status.

02Pop-up on top of pop-up

Every edit opened a dialog that covered the page you were working on.

03Silence after you click

No loading, no success, no error. Waiting looked the same as failing.

Understand · Stage 1 of 3

Legacy audit

The legacy flow made people ask before they could see

01

The page starts empty

The issue

When an admin opens SR-IOV, they see a dropdown and a button. Nothing else. The entire page's instruction is: "Select the required SR-IOV adapter and click Modify." There is no overview, no status, no way to see all adapters at once without opening the list one by one.

02

Every edit happens in a centered modal & nothing tells you what the system is doing

The issue

Want to change an adapter from Shared mode to Dedicated? A modal appears over the page. It shows two radio buttons and grey OK / Cancel buttons. The modal covers the very port table you were just looking at. There's no visual weight to the primary action: OK looks the same as Cancel.

Mode changes, switching an adapter from Shared to Dedicated, are slow operations on the server. They can take time. But none of the legacy screens showed a loading state, a progress indicator, a success confirmation, or an error message. Users clicked OK and waited. They had no way to distinguish "it's running" from "it failed silently."

03

Editing a port takes three steps through a menu with one item

The issue

To modify a physical port: select a radio button → open an "Action" dropdown → click the only item inside it: "Modify Physical Port" → edit in yet another modal. There is also a separate "View" modal and a "Modify" modal for the same port: near-identical content, two different paths, easy to open the wrong one.

  1. 1 Select a radio button
  2. 2 Open "Action"
  3. 3 Click the only item
  4. 4 Edit in another modal
04

The same port has separate View and Modify modals

The issue

Near-identical content in two dialogs; users must learn two paths to one object and may open the wrong one.

4 of the 36 legacy screens are shown here.

Investigate & prioritize · Stage 2 of 3

Sponsor user research

Seven sessions. Real admins.

The project included four discovery sessions and three design-feedback sessions. These weren't exclusively about SR-IOV; they covered the broader feature context. But several signals landed directly on what I was designing.

Before the sessions

AI

Desk research, AI-assisted

Learn. Used IBM BOB and Claude to get up to speed on SR-IOV and how admins use it.

Prepare. Drafted the discussion guide for the generative research.

Probe. Surfaced edge cases early, which later became designed states.

Round one

4

Round one: 4 conversations

Listen. How admins work and how they experience the old screens.

Map. Each person's day-to-day, turned into needs and frustrations.

Scope. Agreed with product managers and engineers what to take on, and why anything was left out.

Round two

3

Round two: 3 feedback sessions

Return. Polished designs, shown to the same people.

Try. We gave them tasks, watched what they did and asked questions.

Improve. What we learned went straight back into the design.

Design & deliver · Stage 3 of 3

Three decisions

Decisions, each traced to its evidence

01

Show all adapters upfront, not behind a dropdown

The solution

The old page was blank until you chose. You couldn't compare adapters, see their status, or understand which one needed attention without working through the dropdown one entry at a time.

The redesign lands directly on a table. All adapters, with their mode, status and location code visible at once.

EvidenceFeedback user 2: "This is definitely better." Users prefer the new view because it surfaces adapter information upfront and makes selection easier.

02

A side panel with sticky Cancel / Save. Design waiting, failing and succeeding

The solution

The redesign opens a right-hand side panel from a selected row. The table stays visible. The Cancel and Save buttons are pinned to the bottom; they never scroll away.

The redesign treats each state as a first-class design problem: skeleton loading, a missing-adapter warning with disabled fields, an in-progress state with a progress bar and estimated duration, and explicit error and success outcomes.

EvidenceFeedback user 3: "This is easier to read and easier to understand."

EvidenceFeedback user 1: "I'm not very happy with the responsiveness... it's complex to see which step the transfer is in." Visibility of progress was the request.

03

Progressive disclosure on the adapter page

The solution

On the adapter page, both sections used to expand by default. This pushed content down and created visual noise.

I chose to expand Physical ports and collapse Logical ports, because research suggested logical-port creation is done at partition level, and admins change them infrequently. Physical ports are the more common working context.

EvidenceResearch-backed data: logical-port creation is done at partition level and admins use this infrequently.

3kinds of hardware view in scope: System, Partition, VIOS

Outcome

What changed for the people using it

Fewer steps

4 → 1
Steps to edit a physical port
Heuristic review

Visible system

0 → 5
Feedback states: loading, missing adapter, in progress, error, success
Heuristic review

One place

Places to view and edit a port
Heuristic review

Visible

You can see what is happening

The old screens stayed silent after a click. Now you see loading, progress, errors and success as they happen.

Findable

You can find things

Adapters used to hide behind a dropdown. Now they are all listed in one table, including their real link speed.

Direct

Fewer clicks

It took a radio button, a one-item menu and a pop-up to reach a port. Now it is one link.

In context

You keep your place

Pop-ups used to cover the table you were editing. A side panel now sits beside it, so the page stays in view.

Consistent

It feels like one product

Two different looks used to be mixed on the same page. Now the buttons, tables and wording match throughout.

Focused

Each port has its own page

Port details used to be buried. Now each port has its own page, so you can see everything about it in one place.

Based on a heuristic review of legacy screens against the redesign. Not a usability test.

Beyond SR-IOV

The side panel and feedback states became shared patterns

Both are now part of the PowerHMC Pattern Library, so other PowerHMC screens use the same edit panel and the same loading, progress, error and success states.

Reflection

What I learned, and what comes next

The lessons I am taking with me, and where this goes after the first release.

What I learned

Build it together

Working closely with Product Managers and Engineering from the start helped me understand what the business needed, what was possible, and how much to take on at once.

Sponsor user research

Admins shaped the design

Admins told us they wanted adapter details up front, clickable IDs and the real link speed. Listening closely paid off.

What I'd do differently

Design the awkward moments sooner

Loading and error screens came late. Next time I would design them right alongside the happy path, not after it.

What's next

Take it further

Bring the same side panel and feedback ideas to the rest of PowerHMC, and check the shipped experience with real users.

Thank you.
